PROBLEM
Orbital data centers can ease power generation concerns on Earth, but
their satellites must be mass and volume efficient for launch and meet
radiative cooling needs. SpaceX's published targets of 250 kW peak / 175
kW average per satellite and 75 kW per ton, with a 100 t Starship launch,
imply 7.5 MW installed peak / 250 kW = 30 satellites.
Why it matters:
AI agents and GPU acceleration allow rapid digital
prototyping; 12 coworking days for an engineer to go from concept to a
chosen mechanical and thermal architecture ready for detailed design.
Why it matters: AI agents and GPU acceleration allow rapid digital prototyping; 12 coworking days for an engineer to go from concept to a chosen mechanical and thermal architecture ready for detailed design.

one Vera Rubin NVL72 (72 GPUs + 36 CPUs); 250 kW peak at
beginning of life. Assumed 640.38 kg payload allocation in a 600 × 1200
× 937 mm box.

Launch fit:
All 30 satellites fit in one Starship: 30 × 3,026 kg = 90.8 t +
2 t dispenser + 7.2 t reserve = 100 t; stowed stack 15.6 m tall in the
modeled 17.24 m payload envelope (≥3.9 mm radial margin).

600 km dawn-dusk sun-synchronous. Arrays face the Sun;

Power: 862 m² solar array; assumed module rating 324.55 W/m² on its remaining planar area; 175 kW in sunlight and a 164.4 kW annual average, including eclipse.
Thermal:
140 radiator panels; coating emissivity 0.92. Fins and tubes
selected by search; modeled glycol-water loop. Cold-plate resistance
assumed for Rubin GPU and HBM.
175 kW in sunlight: rack coolant 339 K to 359 K; Rubin GPU est. 371 K
(target ≈370 K), HBM 373 K (limit 378 K).
250 kW peak (steady state): rack coolant 370 K to 390 K; Rubin GPU est.
410 K, HBM est. 412 K.

Search varied panel count, tubes per panel, fin thickness and array size. 3,048 of 1.81M designs meet every hard limit; lightest with 1 K extra margin chosen, then 1.05M what-if runs co-varied 14 inputs over assumed ranges, not measured probabilities. Radiator emissivity and power conversion efficiency move temperatures most; cold-plate resistance mainly moves the GPU and rack temperature rise mainly moves the coolant.

power conversion efficiency move temperatures most; cold-plate resistance

2  GPU-accelerated design search | GB10
Search, 1.81M designs
0.2136 s
0.5014 s  (2.35×)
7.020 s  (32.9×)

0.1219 s
0.2694 s  (2.21×)
3.792 s  (31.1×)
32.9× faster than one GB10 CPU core; 2.35× faster than all 20 cores.
Versus one core, the GPU pulls ahead above about 1,000 designs and levels off
at 32–33× from about 260,000 designs to the full 1.81M.
Same double-precision math on all; median of 3 runs; timing excludes setup and
compile. GPU: Warp kernels on CUDA. CPU: 1 Arm Cortex-X925 core in the GB10
Grace Blackwell, 1 thread. All cores: the same Warp fp64 code on all 20 cores
(10 X925 + 10 A725), not hand-tuned CPU code.
3  AI fin model check | PhysicsNeMo / Warp
A PhysicsNeMo neural model learns radiator fin efficiency from Warp solver
results (384 training fins), then is checked on 128 fins it never saw, so a fast
learned model can stand in for the solver when screening fin shapes.
Max |Δη| = 9.3e-5.
The chosen design's fins were re-solved with Warp, so no final number rests on
the learned model. A Warp autodiff optimizer, treating panel count and fin size
as continuous, comes within 0.65% of the search's lightest radiator. Its gradients
match finite differences; it is a local check, not a global optimum.

Newton simulates the unfold; Warp re-solves all 21 solar-array hinges (root hinge

hinge parameters.
